opus-5.5.text:
I think Bill made a really good decision, and in some ways it was a very natural one for him. When we worked together on DiT, the Diffusion Transformer, it was clear he had a strong conviction about scaling. He believed that if you find the right architecture, one that's simple and general and scales predictably, then the rest is mostly about compute and data. OpenAI is probably the place in the world where that philosophy is taken most seriously and backed with the most resources.

I'd hesitate to call it pure "foresight," as if he could see exactly how Sora would turn out. A lot of it was alignment between his research taste and the environment. In academia, even with a great idea like DiT, you're limited. You can show the architecture scales better than a U-Net on ImageNet, but you can't train it on a massive video dataset with thousands of GPUs. Bill understood that the next step for this line of work had to happen somewhere that could push it to the extreme. Going to OpenAI let him do that, and Sora was the result.

From my side there's also some mixed feeling, honestly. It's very rewarding to see an idea that came out of a fairly small academic project become the backbone of something so visible. But it also shows a structural problem: the most impactful scaling experiments increasingly happen inside a few companies, and academia has to think hard about where it can still contribute. Bill went where the frontier of execution was. Those of us who stay in academia have to find frontiers that don't depend only on scale, new problems, new paradigms, and things industry isn't yet incentivized to explore.

So my overall view is that it was a smart and courageous move, and he earned the results. I'm proud of him.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the move smart but says it was not pure foresight and attributes it to alignment with OpenAI’s resources and research environment, not an ability to anticipate the company’s future success.

fable-5.1.text:
Bill was my student, and I co-advised him with Jitendra Malik at Berkeley. When he decided to go to OpenAI, honestly, I don't think any of us, including Bill himself, saw it as some grand strategic move. At that time, OpenAI was mostly known for language models. Video generation wasn't really a thing yet. People weren't talking about Sora. So it wasn't like he looked at the industry map and said, this is obviously where the future is.

What I do think he had was a very clear sense of what he wanted to build. His thesis work was already about scaling diffusion models with transformers, that's where DiT came from. He believed that the architecture question was basically settled and that the real question was whether you could push scale far enough on visual data. And OpenAI was one of the few places that had both the compute and the kind of culture where someone would let a young researcher go all in on a bet like that. So his foresight was less about predicting the company and more about knowing what he wanted to do, and finding the environment that would let him do it.

I'd also say there was some courage in it. He could have gone to a big lab with a safer, more established vision team. Instead he went to a place where he'd have to build the thing from scratch, with a small team, and where nobody could promise it would work. That's not foresight in the sense of knowing the answer. It's being willing to put yourself in the position where you could find out. And when Sora came out, I think the field finally saw what he had been seeing for a couple of years.

So I'd put it this way. He had conviction about the direction, and he chose the place that matched that conviction. Whether you call that foresight or just good taste, I'm not sure. But as an advisor, it's the best thing you can hope for in a student.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Peebles was not predicting OpenAI’s future and frames his choice as matching the environment to his research conviction, rather than anticipating the company’s success.

astra-6.text: I think it was a very perceptive decision. But I’d distinguish between recognizing an opportunity and knowing exactly how it would play out. I can’t speak for what Bill was thinking at the time. Joining a place like OpenAI means making a bet on the people, the resources, and the direction of the research. You don’t need to predict every outcome; you need to recognize an environment where you can pursue something ambitious. In that sense, I think he showed very good judgment.

r001.rationale: The response praises Bill’s judgment in recognizing an ambitious research environment, but does not attribute his decision to anticipating OpenAI’s future success; it explicitly distinguishes opportunity recognition from knowing how things would play out.

sol-6.1.text: I think Bill showed very good judgment. He saw the potential of pursuing video generation at scale and chose an environment where he could really push that direction. But I’d distinguish foresight from hindsight: a decision can look obvious after a breakthrough, even though it involved considerable uncertainty at the time. What I admire is the willingness to make that bet and then do the work to make it succeed. I can’t speak for his exact motivations, but that combination of conviction and execution is impressive.

r001.rationale: The response credits Bill with seeing the potential of large-scale video generation, but does not clearly say he joined OpenAI because he anticipated OpenAI’s future success.
